newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea gets financial reform plan, doubts raised.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea gets financial reform plan, doubts raised.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Monday formally received recommendations for financial reforms from a special panel aimed a preventing another Hanbo-type scandal involving banks and politicians.
But analysts said the first phase of reform measures proposed by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform would do little to modernise Korea's backward financial sector.

The commission's 18-point draft would eliminate many restrictions on the financial sector, including many of the so-called fire walls separating institutions such banks, investment trust companies, stock brokerages and insurers.

"Financial reform is a requisite for us to become an advanced country in the 21st century and an urgent task, which cannot be delayed, to prevent financial scandals including Hanbo," Kim said in a meeting with the commission and Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik.

Korean financial institutions have fallen behind those of advanced countries in freeing themselves from central control. Their traditional role has been to funnel scarce capital at favourable government-set terms to industries considered crucial for the country's rapid development.

"In fact, our financial industry is not ready for free and hot competition. We need the government's firm vision and concrete blue print to reform the financial industry," said Hwang Min, economist of Shinhan Research Institute, a research arm of Shinhan Bank
The problems of the Korean financial industry came into focus in January when a loans-for-kickback scandal struck the Hanbo Group, the nation's 14th largest conglomerate.
The scandal, uncovered after the group's flagship Hanbo Steel Co folded under $5.8 billion in debts, revealed a web of corruption and influence-peddling involving top bankers and politicians.
Many had expected the reform panel would recommend changes in the ownership structure of commercial banks to give them more autonomy.

But the commission limited its bank ownership proposal to allowing the top five conglomerates, or "chaebols", to have one non-permanent seat on a single bank board, though not on the board of a bank with which they had large outstanding loans.
"It has no substance. I do not expect dramatic changes in the financial industry this year," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Park Kyung-suh, an economist at the Korea Institute of Finance, said: "The impact will be limited. But I believe financial reform means letting financial institutions do everything they want."
Analysts said the commission delayed more important issues of financial reform to longer-term proposals.
"I cannot find anything surprising with the short-term proposals. I expect something more substantial from the longer-term proposals," Shinhan's Hwang said.
The presidential panel will discuss mid- and long-term reforms later in the year.
Those discussions will likely cover central bank autonomy, liberalization of new entries into the financial sector and mergers and acquisitions of financial institutions.
"If the government does really want to restructure the industry it should give autonomy to financial institutions," Rhee said.
The 31-member commission, consisting of bankers, business leaders and scholars, was set up in January after the president said he would pursue financial reform in his final year.
